title: Income, spending and net worth
objective: Calculate your net worth and monthly surplus from a list of assets, debts, income and bills

q.prompt: Zoe earns $95,000 but owes more than she owns. Tom earns $55,000, has $20,000 saved and no debts. Who is better off **right now**?

options.why: Income is what flows in. What you're worth is what you own minus what you owe.
You can, by comparing what each owns minus what each owes.

q.explanation: A high income doesn't mean wealth. Tom owns more than he owes; Zoe owes more than she owns.

q.prompt: Have a guess: is each one something you **own** or something you **owe**?
q.explanation: Savings and super are things you own (assets). Card balances and loans are money you owe (liabilities).

screens.title: Net worth: own minus owe
screens.body: Add up what you own, your [[assets]]. Subtract what you owe, your [[liabilities]]. What's left is your [[net worth]]. It can be negative, and that's common early on, especially with study or car debt. What matters is which way it's heading.

screens.title: Surplus: in minus out
screens.body: Net worth is a snapshot. Your monthly [[surplus]] is the flow: [[take-home pay]] minus what you spend. A surplus can grow your savings or pay down debt. A deficit means debt is growing or savings are shrinking.

screens.title: Worked example: Aisha, 27, Brisbane
screens.body: Aisha lists everything she owns and owes.

lines: Rent $1,650 + groceries $600 + transport $250 + phone $120 + everything else $780 = **$3,400**
That's $9,600 a year to save or clear debt

q.hint: A liability is money you owe someone else.
q.explanation: A HECS-HELP study loan is money owed, so it's a liability. The account and laptop are assets.

q.prompt: Ella has $2,400 in savings and a car worth $11,000. She owes $8,500 on a car loan and $900 on a card. What's her net worth?
q.hint: Add the two assets, then subtract both debts.

q.sentence: Take-home pay minus spending is your monthly ___.
q.hint: Net worth is a snapshot; this is the monthly flow.
q.explanation: Money left over each month is your surplus. If it's negative, it's a deficit.

q.prompt: A negative net worth means you're bad with money.
q.explanation: Many people start negative because of study or car loans. The direction it's moving matters more than today's number.

q.prompt: Josh takes home $3,600 a month. He spends $1,450 on rent, $520 on food, $180 on transport, $95 on his phone and $600 on everything else. What's his monthly surplus?
q.explanation: Spending totals $2,845, so $3,600 − $2,845 = $755 left each month.

q.prompt: If Josh saved his whole $755 surplus every month, how much would he save in a year?
q.explanation: $755 × 12 = $9,060 a year. Monthly habits look small until you see the yearly total.

q.prompt: Kai pays $500 off his credit card using money from his savings account. What happens to his net worth?

options.why: His debt fell by $500, but his savings fell by $500 too.
He lost $500 of savings but also owes $500 less, so it cancels out.

q.explanation: Assets and liabilities both drop by $500, so net worth doesn't change. He does save on future card interest.

screens.title: Your snapshot
screens.body: Grab your banking app. Jot down roughly what you own and what you owe. No one sees this but you, and a rough number is fine.
screens.action: Write down your **net worth** today, and check it again in three months.

bullets: Net worth = what you own minus what you owe.
Monthly surplus = take-home pay minus spending.
Watch the direction: a growing surplus lifts net worth over time.

reviewBank.prompt: Assets: $3,000 savings and $15,000 super. Liabilities: a $4,500 personal loan. What's the net worth?
Take-home pay is $5,000 a month and spending is $4,350. What's the monthly surplus?
Which of these is a liability?

options.text: A buy now pay later balance

options.why: That's money you own, so it's an asset.
Super belongs to you, so it's an asset.

reviewBank.explanation: Anything you still have to pay back, like a BNPL balance, is a liability.
